brief.t: China has a smaller crop (7.26 mt, -2.0%), yarn imports +54% and cotton imports +71% y/y, domestic lint 1,790 yuan/t under the target price and 1,987 yuan/t over landed imports. Supply is not the constraint and imported fibre is cheap, so Chinese prices should hold a premium to the world but struggle to rally while new-crop sales are heavy; strong yarn imports are the main channel through which China adds to world cotton demand this year.

The China Cotton Association's latest survey (2026-09) puts the 2026 crop at **7.26 mt** (-2.0% vs last season's CCA final of 7.41 mt), +109 kt vs the previous survey; area 43.69 m mu (2.91 m ha), yield 166.2 kg/mu (2,493 kg/ha). From the same survey month to the association's final number, past seasons moved -1.0% to +13.5% (median +0.0%, 7 seasons): that points to a final of **7.26 mt** (range 7.19–8.25). In the 2 seasons with a published final figure it came in above the September survey (2024 +13.5%, 2025 +1.9%), so the risk skews up. USDA has 7.29 mt (33.5 m bales); compare the agencies' revisions rather than their levels.

Xinjiang picking 67.0% at 10-15 (+9.5 pts vs last year, +13.7 vs the 4-season average); National picking 17.3% at 09-30 (+12.2 pts vs last year, +8.7 vs the 5-season average); National seed-cotton selling 12.6% at 09-30 (+10.8 pts vs last year, +9.2 vs the 5-season average); Xinjiang selling 60.0% at 10-15 (+19.9 pts vs last year, +32.5 vs the 5-season average). A fast harvest brings new-crop lint to market early: ginning and hedge selling on Zhengzhou come forward, which usually weighs on nearby prices in Oct–Dec. Farmers' seed-cotton price 7.4 yuan/kg (+16.9% y/y) in the 2026-10-10 survey.

Jan–Sep 2026 cotton yarn imports **1,600 kt** (+53.8% y/y, +32.9% vs the 5-year average; #2 of 6 years) and raw cotton **1,160 kt** (+70.6% y/y, -21.1% vs average). Counting yarn as lint (×1.1), China has taken 2,920 kt of foreign fibre through Sep vs 1,824 kt a year ago; yarn is 60% of it. Imported yarn averages $2,371/t (+6.6% y/y).

Yarn is coming in much faster than raw cotton: mills and weavers are buying foreign yarn (mainly Vietnam, India, Pakistan, Uzbekistan) instead of spinning domestic lint. Downstream fabric demand is there, but the import-quota and price structure favour yarn; this is demand for cotton outside China's quota system and it caps Chinese spinners' margins; raw cotton imports have recovered from last year's low base as the domestic premium over world prices widened and extra sliding-scale quota was issued; imported lint is 1,987 yuan/t below the domestic price at 1% duty, so mills with quota have every reason to import; the binding limit is quota, which is why foreign yarn (no quota) fills the gap.

China's extra yarn is cotton spun elsewhere: Vietnam +235 kt of yarn ≈ +1.19 m bales of lint (+14% of its USDA imports; ≈+0.40 m bales of US cotton at the usual 34% US share); India +173 kt of yarn ≈ +0.87 m bales of lint (spins mostly its own cotton); Pakistan +41 kt of yarn ≈ +0.21 m bales of lint (+4% of its USDA imports; ≈+0.08 m bales of US cotton at the usual 38% US share); Uzbekistan +27 kt of yarn ≈ +0.14 m bales of lint (spins mostly its own cotton). That supports US and Brazilian sales to Vietnam and the South Asian importers even while China's own lint imports are slow; India and Uzbekistan mainly turn their own crops into yarn, which tightens their exportable cotton instead. Country split is an estimate (CCFGroup insight 2026-10-23 (China customs HS 5205), 2026-09).

USDA has China importing 1.52 mt (7.0 m bales) in 2026/27 (Aug–Jul). Aug–Sep arrivals were 130 kt, 8% of that; in the last 5 seasons 9–23% (median 12%) had arrived by the end of Sep, so the pace points to about 1.04 mt. For 2025/26 customs shows 1.58 mt against USDA's 1.58 mt, so USDA tracks customs closely once the year is done. Read: on pace alone USDA looks about 2.2 m bales high (two months is a weak guide: the share by now has ranged 9–23%), and it holds only if buying picks up when the 2027 quota is issued in January; early arrivals are slow because this year's quota is used up, the domestic crop is early and large, and mills are importing yarn instead. USDA's own balance leaves China's 2026/27 stocks-to-use at 82.5%, the lowest since 2020/21 (81.7%, when imports were 2.79 mt); restoring 85% needs about 1.0 m bales more stock. Policy can change this. Extra sliding-scale quota was issued in 8 of the last 9 years (2018 800 kt, 2019 800 kt, 2020 400 kt, 2021 700 kt, 2022 400 kt, 2023 750 kt, 2025 200 kt, 2026 300 kt); the one skip, 2024, came when reserve restocking had already lifted imports. The state reserve sold 409 kt from 07/2026 to 09/2026, 332 kt of it imported cotton. After the 2023 sale (880 kt) the reserve restocked mostly with imports in 2023/24, about 3 m bales above the prior year. Pace plus replacing the imported cotton it just sold gives about 1.37 mt (6.3 m bales); an early 2027 sliding-scale quota would add more (the pace already reflects a typical year's quota, so count only an unusually large one). So USDA's number needs restocking or extra quota, and history says at least one usually comes; watch the reserve's purchase announcements and the 2027 quota. USDA's mill use is 9.14 mt (42.0 m bales, +1.0%) vs the CCA's 8.92 mt. Yarn imports Aug–Sep are 390 kt vs 260 kt a year earlier (+50%): every tonne of imported yarn is about 1.1 t of lint that Chinese mills do not spin, so a mill-use increase looks optimistic while yarn imports run this high; China's fibre demand is real but it is being met offshore, which helps exporters that sell to Vietnam, Pakistan and India more than those selling lint to China.

CCA balance sheet 2026/27: production 7.26 mt, imports 1.50, mill use 8.92, ending stocks 6.21 mt (stocks/use 70%); mill use +1.7% vs 2025/26 and stocks -170 kt. Mill use exceeds the crop by 1.66 mt, covered by lint imports (1.50 mt) and stocks. Imported yarn comes on top of this: it is weavers' demand that bypasses Chinese spinners (calendar 2025: 1,500 kt of yarn, ≈1.65 mt of lint), so China's total cotton use is larger than the mill-use line suggests.

CCIndex 3128B 16,810 yuan/t on 2026-10-29 = **114.4¢/lb** (105.0¢ ex-VAT) at USD/CNY 6.665; that is 1,790 yuan/t (-9.6%) below the 18,600 yuan/t Xinjiang target price (126.6¢/lb); at the harvest-season average so far (17,536) the target-price payment would be about 1,064 yuan/t, paid to Xinjiang growers, so it supports planting rather than the lint price; Zhengzhou cotton (CF front) 15,165 yuan/t = 103.2¢/lb vs ICE 78.15¢ (+16.5¢ ex-VAT; 61st percentile since 2017); Cotlook A 89.70¢ (2026-10-28) lands at 14,923 yuan/t inside the 1% quota and 15,259 under sliding-scale quota, so imported cotton is 1,987 / 1,651 yuan/t cheaper than domestic 3128B; Zhengzhou yarn minus cotton 5,910 yuan/t vs a 5-year average of 6,295 (a rough spinning margin).

Shankar-6 (CAI spot, Gujarat 29 mm) 67,000 Rs/candy on 2026-10-28 = **89.8¢/lb** at 95.2 Rs/$ (+27% y/y in rupees); Cotlook A 89.7¢, ICE 78.2¢, China 3128B 105.0¢ ex-VAT. The 2026/27 MSP (kapas 8,267/8,667 Rs/quintal medium/long) implies lint at roughly 64,500 Rs/candy (86¢/lb; 34% lint out-turn, seed credited at Rs 35/kg, ginning Rs 1,500/candy), so Indian lint is above the support level: CCI buying at MSP sets the floor and keeps Indian cotton out of export competition unless world prices rise.

Brent 111$ (+2% in 6 months) has pushed PTA +2% and polyester staple fibre +2% to 8,608 yuan/t (59¢/lb, 54¢ ex-VAT), while Zhengzhou cotton moved -8%. Cotton now costs 1.76× polyester in China, 0th percentile since PSF futures listed (range 1.76–3.19, average 2.20; 1.96 six months ago). ICE cotton is 1.45× Chinese PSF ex-VAT (average 1.92). Cotton is unusually cheap against polyester: spinners shift blends toward cotton when the ratio is this low, which adds to cotton use with a lag of a few months, provided crude stays high; polyester capacity is ample, so the PSF rally depends on oil rather than tight fibre supply. Weekly PSF and Brent changes correlate 0.55 over three years.
Jan–Sep 2026 imports, customs: soybeans 86.1 mt (-0%), corn 2.1 mt (+127%), wheat 3.8 mt (+28%), barley 11.4 mt (+46%), sorghum 6.4 mt (+76%).
